qs.q: A clinician plans the initial diagnostic evaluation for a 2-year-old child with unexplained global developmental delay. Thyroid function testing is routinely included in this work-up primarily for which reason?
o: It identifies a treatable metabolic condition
qs.e: Thyroid function tests are performed because congenital hypothyroidism is a treatable metabolic cause of developmental delay. It is distinct from chromosomal disorders like fragile X syndrome which cannot be reversed by hormone replacement.

o: Two or more areas before age five
qs.e: It requires delay in two or more domains before age 5. The other options do not meet the definition.

qs.q: A 2-year-old child presents with global developmental delay and delayed attainment of milestones. Which of the following clinical features warrants proceeding directly to cerebral magnetic resonance imaging?
qs.e: Focal neurological signs, seizures, or regression are clear indications for neuroimaging in developmental delay. Isolated speech delay or a family history of learning difficulties rarely requires immediate brain imaging.

exam: What bedside questions differentiate GDD from isolated language disorder? — Ask about motor milestones, social interaction, and any regression; language delay alone lacks motor/social lag.
A 3‑year‑old with GDD and fever has a normal CSF Gram stain. What is your next step? — Consider TB meningitis; start empiric anti‑TB therapy if resources limit culture.
How would you prioritize investigations when MRI is unavailable? — Use head ultrasound (if fontanelle open), basic labs, and clinical neuro‑exam to guide management.
Why is zinc supplementation recommended in many GDD cases in East Africa? — Zinc deficiency impairs neurodevelopment; supplementation is low‑cost and improves growth.
A child with GDD tests HIV‑positive. Which antiretroviral class should be avoided and why? — Avoid stavudine because it can cause peripheral neuropathy, worsening motor delay.
What red‑flag symptom mandates urgent referral to a tertiary centre? — New onset seizures or rapid developmental regression.

Explain how you would counsel caregivers about realistic goals for a child with severe GDD. — Emphasize functional independence, use of assistive devices, and regular therapy; set measurable short‑term milestones.

What distinguishes GDD caused by congenital hypothyroidism from that caused by chronic malnutrition? — Hypothyroidism presents with prolonged jaundice, coarse facial features, and elevated TSH; malnutrition shows wasting, micronutrient deficiencies, and normal thyroid labs.
ai.title: Global Developmental Delay
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Global developmental delay (GDD) is a significant lag in two or more developmental domains in children under five. Diagnosis relies on age‑appropriate milestones, careful history, and targeted investigations, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Use locally validated milestone charts (e.g., WHO child growth and development standards).
Exclude isolated intellectual disability without broader domain delay.
sections.p: GDD is defined as performance >2 standard deviations below the mean in at least two of the five domains: gross motor, fine motor, language, cognition, and social‑emotional, in a child younger than 5 years.

b: Mild: 2–3 SD below mean, child can perform basic self‑care.
Moderate: 3–4 SD below, requires assistance for most activities.
Severe: >4 SD below, profound dependence on caregivers.
sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of delay and functional impact:

b: Prenatal: maternal infections (CMV, rubella, HIV), malnutrition, toxin exposure.
Perinatal: birth asphyxia, prematurity, neonatal meningitis.
Post‑natal: untreated severe malaria, TB meningitis, HIV encephalopathy, chronic malnutrition, lead poisoning, untreated hypothyroidism.
sections.p: Causes are grouped into prenatal, perinatal, and post‑natal factors; in East Africa, infectious and nutritional etiologies dominate.

b: Gross motor lag: not walking by 18 months.
Language lag: <10 words by 24 months.
Social‑emotional: limited eye contact, poor response to name.
sections.p: Parents notice delayed sitting, crawling, speech, or social interaction compared with peers. Red flags include regression, seizures, or failure to thrive.
Prioritise tests that are feasible locally; if unavailable, rely on clinical clues and refer.

t.b: Detect anemia, electrolyte imbalance, infection; normal results do not exclude chronic infection.
Identify nutritional deficiencies common in low‑resource settings; low levels support malnutrition‑related GDD.
Screen for HIV encephalopathy; positive result directs antiretroviral therapy.
Look for pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein; if lumbar puncture unavailable, treat empirically for TB meningitis.
Detect congenital or acquired hypothyroidism; treatable cause of GDD.

t.a: Head ultrasound (if fontanelle open) or MRI (if referral possible)
t.b: Identify structural brain lesions; if imaging unavailable, base decisions on neuro‑exam and history.

b: Seizure onset or status epilepticus.
Rapid regression of milestones.
Severe malnutrition (weight‑for‑height <‑3 SD).
Signs of intracranial infection (fever, neck stiffness).
Infectious cause: appropriate antibiotics/antituberculars; avoid aminoglycosides if renal function impaired.
Nutritional rehab: high‑energy, protein‑rich diet; zinc supplementation.
HIV: start ART per national guidelines; avoid stavudine in children with neuropathy.
Hypothyroidism: levothyroxine (dose titrated by TSH).
Early intervention: physiotherapy, speech therapy, caregiver education.
sections.p: Treat underlying cause, then provide multidisciplinary support.

b: Re‑assess milestones every 3 months.
Screen for vision/hearing deficits annually.
Vaccinate per EPI schedule; prevent malaria with insecticide‑treated nets.
sections.p: Regular monitoring of growth, development, and treatment response.

b: Intellectual disability alone – global delay involves multiple domains early, not just cognition.
Autism spectrum disorder – social‑communication deficits predominate, motor milestones often normal.
Specific language disorder – isolated speech delay without motor or social impairment.
